blocks.text: Where a financial analyst's week really goes

Most public data on analyst time is thin. The best job-specific source is the APEX survey, which asked 227 experts about their work. Of those, 58 were financial or investment analysts. The answers are self-reported, and the survey date is not stated, so read the numbers as a rough guide.

blocks.caption: APEX survey, self-reported. Shares as published.

blocks.text: Read that table with care. Core activities, including financial modeling, take 47.2% of the week in that sample. Financial modeling is only one part of core work. The survey puts it at 23.5% of core activities, not of the whole week.

Microsoft's 2023 Work Trend Index points the same way for a wider group. The heaviest email users, the top 25%, spend 8.8 hours a week on email. The heaviest meeting users spend 7.5 hours a week in meetings. Those figures cover commercial workers in general, not analysts.

Microsoft also says the average employee spends 57% of their time communicating. That figure comes from Microsoft 365 app usage over a 28-day period ending March 2023, not from a survey. It is a weak guide to your own calendar and inbox.

Analyst time matters because the role is large and well paid. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics lists a median pay of $103,570 a year and 443,100 jobs in 2025. Its page describes modeling, reports and presentations, but it does not mention spreadsheets or email.
How much time goes to typing and data clean-up
I could not find a source that measures how long analysts spend typing or cleaning data. Most figures you see online come without a method. Measure it yourself before you buy anything.

Try a simple log for five working days. Keep a note on your Mac and write each task down in 30-minute blocks. At the end of the week, add up three buckets: model work, communication, and everything else. That gives you your own baseline, and it shows where an assistant would help.
Where an AI assistant for financial analysts fits

An AI assistant for financial analysts earns its place in the small gaps. It answers the questions that stop you for longer than they should. Where is that input? What does this error mean? How do I format this range? Those questions take seconds to ask. Looking for the answers yourself costs far more.

Lazur works that way. You hold ⌥ ⌘, ask out loud, and Lazur looks at your screen and answers out loud. If you ask where something is, it draws a circle and a label around it. If you ask how to do something, it guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. For more on Excel, see [Excel for financial analysts on Mac](/for/financial-analysts/excel).
Dictation for call notes, memos and snippets

Hold fn to dictate. Lazur turns your speech into clean, formatted text at the cursor, in any app. You can save snippets, add terms to a personal dictionary, and use clipboard slots. Dictation is unlimited on both the Pro and Power plans.

Snippets suit the text you type every week. Think of a standard footnote, a call summary template, or the sentence you always write when a covenant is close to its limit. Save each one once, so you never retype it from memory.
Speech tools mishear tickers, share classes and decimals. Read every number back before it goes into a model or a memo. A wrong digit is cheap to fix in dictation and expensive once a client sees it.
Mistakes analysts make with AI assistants

items: Pasting client or deal data into a tool your firm has not approved. Check the policy first.
Trusting a formula explanation without tracing it. Click into the cell and test one input.
Asking a broad question about the whole model. Ask about one cell, one error or one label.
Treating a research summary as a source. Open the original filing before you cite it.
Forgetting that Lazur sees only what is on screen. Put the relevant cells in view first.
Skipping the trial test. Run one real task in the trial before you pay.

blocks.text: The common thread is trust without a check. An answer is a lead, not a sign-off. Click into the cell, test the logic on one input, and compare the output with a number you already trust.
Confidential data, deal news and your firm's rules

Financial analysts often hold information that is confidential or not yet public. Your firm sets the rules for where that data can go. Follow those rules before anything else. Lazur sends audio and the screenshot to AI providers to answer you, and those are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

Those facts do not decide the question for your job. Ask your compliance team which AI tools are allowed, and what they say about client identifiers, model files and material non-public information. This page makes no compliance claims for Lazur. Your employer decides what fits.
A safe way to start is public data. Use a public filing, a sample model with invented numbers, or a published earnings call transcript. Move to live deal work only after your compliance team agrees.
Excel and Google Sheets on a Mac: where help is most useful

Many analysts build their core models in Excel. No source I opened names Excel as the most used tool for analysts, so treat that as a working assumption. Some teams use Google Sheets for shared comps and quick trackers. It runs in Chrome or Safari.

On a Mac, most Excel shortcuts use ⌘. Microsoft announced KeyTips for Word, Excel, PowerPoint and OneNote for Mac on June 21, 2024. You press Option to show the letter hints on the ribbon. That was a preview for Beta Channel builds, and I could not confirm its current status, so check your version under Excel > About Excel.

Row limits matter when you pull large data. A worksheet holds up to 1,048,576 rows and 16,384 columns, according to Microsoft's specifications page. That page does not say whether those limits apply to Excel for Mac, so test a large file before you rely on it.

Microsoft's October 2026 Excel update says some Copilot skills are rolling out to general availability on all platforms, including Mac. The skill recorder is still Insider-only on Mac. Lazur is a separate app and is not an add-in for Excel or any other app.

For Google Sheets, a common fix is a dropdown list for scenario names. The steps are in [how to create a dropdown list in Google Sheets on Mac](/how-to/create-a-dropdown-list-in-google-sheets). Ask Lazur to guide you through it, and it waits for each click before the next step.
Worked example: a broken reference before the morning call

Say your comps tab shows a reference error in H22 at 08:40. Someone deleted a row that the formula used. Ask out loud what the error in H22 means. If the formula bar is on screen, Lazur reads the formula and explains which reference broke.

Then fix it yourself. Click into the formula, find the reference, and point it at the right row. Lazur explains and points. You make the edit. Check the result against the number you expect, then send the file.
What to check before you use an AI answer

items: Confirm the cell or range in the answer is the one you are looking at.
Test the logic on one simple input you can check by hand.
Compare the output with a number from a source you trust.
Read every number, date and ticker back once.
Note any answer that changed a model, so you can trace it later.

faq.question: Does Lazur run inside Excel or Google Sheets?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. It is not a plugin or add-in for any app, and it has no partnership with any app maker. It sees your screen while you hold the shortcut, and it answers out loud.

faq.question: Does Lazur edit my spreadsheet or click buttons for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. When you ask how to do something, it guides you one click at a time and waits for each click. You make each change yourself.

faq.question: Can I use an AI assistant with confidential deal data?
faq.answer: Check your firm's rules first. Lazur sends audio and a screenshot to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your compliance team decides whether that fits your work. This page makes no compliance claims for Lazur.

faq.question: How accurate are the answers about formulas?
faq.answer: Treat them as a starting point. Lazur can explain a formula when it is on screen. Test the explanation on one input, and check the result against a number you trust. An answer can sound right and still be wrong for your model.

faq.question: What does the trial cost?
faq.answer: Lazur has a 3-day Pro trial with no credit card. The trial starts when you first open the app. After that, Pro is $18 a month, or $15 a month billed annually, with 250 AI actions. Dictation is unlimited on both Pro and Power.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS, on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available.

faq.question: Which Excel features are current on a Mac?
faq.answer: It depends on your version. Microsoft's October 2026 Excel update says some Copilot skills reach general availability on Mac, while the skill recorder stays Insider-only on Mac. Check your build under Excel > About Excel, and read Microsoft's What's New page for the features that apply to it.

faq.question: Does the Option key show Excel shortcuts on a Mac?
faq.answer: Microsoft announced KeyTips for Mac in June 2024. You press Option to show the letter hints on the ribbon. That announcement described a Beta preview, so check that your build shows them before you rely on them.

painPoints.title: Meetings and email eat the hours
painPoints.text: Public data suggests meetings and communication take a large share of the week. In the APEX sample, investment banking analysts spent 14.7% of work time in meetings and 13.5% on communications. That leaves less room for the model you were hired to build.

painPoints.title: Small questions stop you
painPoints.text: A missing input, a broken reference or an unfamiliar function can cost a long stretch of time. You search, scroll and ask a colleague. Much of that time goes to finding the answer, not to the analysis behind it.

painPoints.title: Clean-up before the real work
painPoints.text: Data arrives with stray spaces, merged cells or dates stored as text. You reformat it before you model anything. No source I opened measures how long this takes, so track it for a week to get your own number.

painPoints.title: Writing the same text again
painPoints.text: Call summaries, footnotes and follow-up notes repeat from deal to deal. You type the same paragraph many times. Snippets and dictation cover much of it, but only after you set them up once.
